title: I still can't use Google's best Gemini model on my $20 AI Pro plan
excerpt: So much for being an 'AI Pro' plan
content_html:
Published Nov 23, 2026, 8:45 AM EST

I've been writing about Android since 2011, with a focus on device reviews, Samsung and Google Pixel hardware, Google’s apps and services, and Gemini AI. Throughout my writing career, I've reviewed several Android phones and attended major consumer tech events like MWC and IFA.

Carrying both a Samsung or Pixel flagship and an iPhone as daily drivers gives me deep insight into how Android works and how it compares to iOS. I also closely follow Google’s AI efforts, exploring how Gemini fits into Android and the wider Google ecosystem.

I have been writing for Android Police since 2021, covering news, how-tos, and features. You can find my previous work on Neowin, AndroidBeat, Times of India, iPhoneHacks, MySmartPrice, and MakeUseOf.

When not working, I tend to mindlessly scroll through X, play with new AI models, or go on long road trips. You can reach out to me on X or drop me an email at rajesh@androidpolice.com.

After over a year of disappointing AI models, Google has finally given me enough reasons to get excited about Gemini.

In a short span, it has released Argon, Carbon, and now Neon, promising better reasoning, more capable coding, and the ability to tackle increasingly complicated tasks.

But despite subscribing to Google's $20-a-month AI Pro plan, I still can't try everything the company is showing off. If anything, it makes me feel like my Gemini subscription isn't worth it for its AI features.

Pro pricing, second-class treatment

Paying $20 a month still leaves you looking up at Ultra

Claude, ChatGPT, and many other AI providers offer a $ 20-a-month AI plan.

Of them, Google's AI Pro plan probably offers the most benefits, bundling up to 5 TB of cloud storage, deep Gemini integration across Google's apps, and more. If you're already deep in Google's ecosystem, this subscription makes a lot of sense.

That's what attracted me to Google's AI Pro plan. A year ago, I cared less about the latest Gemini model and more about the extra cloud storage and other perks. That was because Gemini's coding and reasoning capabilities were behind the competition.

Over the last year, though, I started relying more on ChatGPT and Claude and started dabbling in vibe coding. Now, with Google catching up with its latest round of Gemini 4 models (Argon, Carbon, and Neon), I was excited to put my AI Pro subscription to full use.

It was time for the "AI" in my Google AI Pro subscription to live up to its name. But Google, being Google, could not make this straightforward.

Take Carbon, Google's strongest model for complex coding, debugging, and demanding research. Think of it as the company's answer to Claude's Fable and ChatGPT's Astra.

As I have used the other two models, I was interested in trying Carbon to see what improvements Google's cutting-edge AI models offer and what I could build with them.

But Google restricted Carbon access in Antigravity, the Gemini app, and AI Mode in Search to AI Ultra subscribers, leaving AI Pro subscribers out. My $20-a-month Pro subscription wasn't enough.

So, to try Google's latest AI model in the Gemini app, I needed to pay $100 a month. Unlike Claude or ChatGPT, my existing subscription didn't let me try the model with limited usage or for a few days to see whether it would make a meaningful difference to my work.

Carbon is also available through Google's paid API, so Ultra isn't the only way to access it. But that requires separate billing and a different workflow. It doesn't solve the frustration of paying for Gemini and still needing to spend more to test its flagship model.

I don't expect unlimited access to every model for $20 a month. Higher usage limits and the ability to run lengthy, demanding tasks are reasonable benefits for Ultra subscribers.

But a small Carbon allowance would let Pro users test Google's claims with their own prompts before deciding whether to upgrade.

Gemini is not known for its coding and reasoning capabilities, so I will blindly upgrade to the $100 Ultra plan just to try its latest model.

And sometimes, even paying for Ultra doesn't get you access when Google first announces a model.

Announced today, available another day

Even the expensive plan comes with a wait

Worse, upgrading to the $100 AI Ultra plan will not get me day-one access to Gemini's latest models. Google announced Argon on September 30, but limited access to trusted cybersecurity defenders through its Fairwind program.

Developers and consumers had to wait until October 13 for broader availability. Carbon followed the same pattern, with an October 28 announcement and a November 10 release.

That wait also kills the excitement of a new Gemini model release. When OpenAI or Anthropic launch a new model, my social media feeds buzz with people showing what they have built, comparing results, and finding improvements beyond the typical benchmarks.

Those examples make me want to open ChatGPT or Claude and try the new model myself to see how it would improve my workflow.

That's not the case with a new Gemini model launch. When access is restricted, there is less opportunity to join in and discover what the model can do. By the time Google opens up wider access, I have lost the urge to experiment and gone back to the tools I already use.

Give Pro users a reason to stay

Google has Gemini models that make me want to try them over ChatGPT and Claude. But that means little when the company does not provide easy access despite paying for its $20 AI plan.

I don't need unlimited access to Carbon for every future flagship Gemini model. Even a small allowance would be good enough.

Until then, AI Pro remains a subscription I'll use only for its storage and extras.
